summary: The bill amends the Bankruptcy Code to require oil, gas, and coal companies in bankruptcy to pay all environmental cleanup and reclamation costs before other claims, by treating those costs as priority expenses that cannot be discharged, barring asset abandonment, extending the fraudulent-transfer look-back period, and allowing courts to claw back executive pay or impose liability on parent companies, private equity, and hedge funds if funds are short.

scores.thoughts: The bill amends bankruptcy code provisions for fossil fuel companies to prioritize environmental reclamation costs. It contains no provisions that authorize, appropriate, or alter any form of federal government spending.
The bill makes no changes to tax law, tax rates, deductions, or liabilities.
No provisions relate to healthcare delivery, insurance, or regulation.
The bill has no connection to firearms or gun regulations.
No immigration-related content appears in the bill.
The legislation does not address reproductive rights or abortion access.
No references to military or defense spending or policy.

The core purpose of the bill is to strengthen environmental accountability for fossil fuel companies in bankruptcy by (1) elevating reclamation costs above most other claims, (2) making environmental obligations non-dischargeable, (3) prohibiting abandonment of polluting assets, and (4) extending look-back periods for fraudulent transfers. These changes directly expand the enforceability of environmental cleanup requirements under multiple federal environmental statutes.
The bill does not modify any welfare, nutrition, housing, or income-support programs.
No education policy or funding provisions are present.
The bill contains nothing related to drug enforcement or decriminalization.
No sentencing, policing, or criminal-procedure reforms are included.
The legislation does not address tariffs, trade agreements, or import/export rules.
The bill does not alter federal deficit or debt-management policy.
No provisions touch on LGBTQ legal protections or rights.
Foreign assistance programs are unaffected.
The bill has no bearing on voting access or election administration.
No technology, data, or privacy regulations are addressed.

While the bill gives non-executive employee wages a higher priority than reclamation costs in fossil-fuel bankruptcies, this is a narrow, technical adjustment within bankruptcy priority rules and does not alter broader labor or union law.
The legislation does not engage with religious exemptions or anti-discrimination rules.
